name: Phragmites

project_scope.scope: Existing canonical species only; no new admission

look_here_first: COMMON REED (Phragmites): a tall rhizomatous wetland GRASS with jointed stems, long blades, and enormous silky branched plumes. But DO NOT equate species name with invasive: North American native subsp. americanus, Eurasian introduced lineage (often subsp. australis), and Gulf Coast subsp. berlandieri/cryptogenic lineage all occur in the broader Texas region. Inspect real SHEATH, STEM, LIGULE and ripe GLUMES before assigning lineage; Texas state-level native presence does not prove Hays County occurrence.

recognition.where_to_look_first: COMMON REED (Phragmites): a tall rhizomatous wetland GRASS with jointed stems, long blades, and enormous silky branched plumes. But DO NOT equate species name with invasive: North American native subsp. americanus, Eurasian introduced lineage (often subsp. australis), and Gulf Coast subsp. berlandieri/cryptogenic lineage all occur in the broader Texas region. Inspect real SHEATH, STEM, LIGULE and ripe GLUMES before assigning lineage; Texas state-level native presence does not prove Hays County occurrence.
priority: Recognize common reed (Phragmites australis) as a tall wetland perennial with jointed reed culms and feathery spreading flower head
Rule out tall grass look-alikes Arundo donax (giant reed) and Zizaniopsis miliacea (giant cutgrass) using flowering spikelet structure
Examine several same-plant mature stem internodes and leaf sheath attachment (loose/caducous versus tight/persistent)
Measure true ligule at the blade/sheath collar on mature green culm with 1-mm scale; compare typical 1.0–1.7 mm native against 0.4–0.9 mm introduced
Inspect measured mature lower and upper glumes and lemma to corroborate without forcing from overlap
Consider Gulf Coast berlandieri, historical taxonomy/provenance and DNA if management decisions depend on lineage

comparison_lesson.title: Phragmites: common reed is not automatically an exotic
comparison_lesson.memory_rule: Phragmites species-ID FIRST; lineage SECOND. Native americanus, introduced Eurasian australis and Gulf Coast berlandieri are distinct management questions.
quick_split: Species: common reed has big feathery panicles, jointed rhizomatous reed canes and multi-flowered hairy-rachilla spikelets; compare to Arundo donax and Zizaniopsis miliacea.
Native americanus (Texas state-level presence): older leaf sheaths often fall away leaving exposed glossy smooth often reddish stems, ligule about 1.0–1.7 mm, generally longer glumes.
Introduced Eurasian lineage: sheaths generally remain tightly attached on older stems; internodes tend dull and ridged, ligule about 0.4–0.9 mm and somewhat shorter glumes.

Gulf Coast berlandieri: also occurs in Texas; cryptogenic/uncertain origin in USGS literature while Kew marks it native to Texas; don't force native americanus versus Eurasian using two traits if a third lineage is plausible.
guardrails: Never equate the species name Phragmites australis with an invasive management conclusion.
USGS/USDA and Kew treatment of Gulf Coast berlandieri origins differ; species-level presence is not Hays County subspecies provenance.
At least 3–4 characters on SAME specimen or genotype/voucher are needed where management depends on lineage.
Panicle density, height, red stem color, shoot density and habitat alone are not proof. Native forms can make substantial reed stands.
No separate canonical species card for the three subspecies: they are comparison concepts only, never auto-admitted or used in native county metrics.
Do not propose herbicide, cutting or removal until introduced status independently established and local management plan reviewed.

what_to_teach_crew: The plant Phragmites australis has both native and introduced lineages in Texas; never automatically classify a big reed colony as invasive.
Photograph the stand, culm, sheath, node, collar/ligule and ripe spikelets of the SAME plant; keep a location record for later review.
Watch mature older SHEATHS: loose or dropping can support native americanus; retained tightly attached can support introduced, but neither stands alone.
Measure actual LIGULE and both GLUMES under magnification; do not treat the Austrian photo of a fringed collar as a measured North American native/invasive individual.
A third Gulf Coast lineage (berlandieri) complicates Texas work. Treat as lineage UNRESOLVED until verified, especially when management would remove plants.
Compare giant reed Arundo donax and native giant cutgrass Zizaniopsis miliacea so the crew first knows it is common reed.
visual_needs: Whole reed colony, flowering panicle and wetland habitat with scale; compare stand structure but do not decide native from density
SAME LIVE culm near mid-stem: shiny or ridged exposed internode with node, aging leaf sheath wrapped or gaping, and true collar
5–10 intact ligules measured next to 1-mm rule under 10–20×; photo identifies actual blade/sheath junction and hair fringe
Five ripe matched lower and upper glumes detached with accurate 1-mm ruler; annotate each glume separately
Silky spikelet/rachilla hairs, fertile lemma and flowering head macros; compare Arundo donax and Zizaniopsis miliacea
Document locality and collect voucher or DNA/haplotype evidence for disputed Gulf / native / Eurasian lineages BEFORE treatment

items.label: Common reed — real source photo
items.image_role: Existing physically present species-labelled JPEG visually inspected; only gross structure markers certified
items.caption: COMMON REED: robust very tall jointed perennial stems, long broad leaves, underground rhizomes and enormous silver-tan feathery panicles. CRITICAL: Phragmites australis includes native North American and invasive introduced lineages. Do not identify lineage from this single photo or decide on treatment without native/introduced subspecies evaluation. Collar/lemma/rhizome characters are not visible in this source photo.
items.why_it_matters: Arundo donax (giant reed) has bamboo-like robust stems, frequently wide leaves and different denser seedhead spikelets; Zizaniopsis miliacea (giant cutgrass) is another tall native wetland grass with a more open panicle and different spikelets. To distinguish Phragmites native vs introduced, compare multi-character sheath, leaf, culm and glume traits and ideally genetics/provenance; never a single seedhead.

items.label: Native American reed — reddish exposed stem and loose sheath
items.image_role: Michigan source-identified native-lineage photo. Compare exposed reddish glossy internode and aging sheath: NOT a Texas or Hays specimen.
items.caption: The reddish exposed internode and pale sheath wrapping above it are visible on this species-labelled Michigan specimen. The older sheath junction is apparent. The photo alone cannot prove lineage or an exact ligule measurement; use several anatomy characters together.
items.why_it_matters: Teaches a practical native-lineage candidate character: later-season exposed reddish shiny stems after older leaf sheaths loosen. Eurasian introduced forms generally keep sheaths tightly attached, but phenology overlaps.
items.creator: Sheila Collins Bourgoin (sheila5)
items.photo_status: Real licensed Wikimedia image visually inspected 2026-10-21; marked only visible sheath and red stem. Original iNaturalist determination remains provisional; Michigan, not Texas. Do NOT infer a precise 1–1.7 mm ligule from image.

items.label: Native American reed — winter stand with exposed reddish canes
items.image_role: Michigan labelled native reed population in winter, with exposed leafless reed stems; no reproductive dissections
items.caption: Winter source-labelled native reed stand shows a mixture of exposed pale and red-brown cane-like stems among winter-dried vegetation. Less dense than some introduced populations but stand density alone is not proof of lineage.
items.why_it_matters: Provides a seasonal habitat view of source-identified native reeds for crews inspecting mature fall/winter stems and leaf-sheath shedding.

items.label: Common reed ligule — actual fringe at leaf collar
items.image_role: Austrian reed photographed in Europe; leaf sheath/collar and actual hair fringe visible with source 5-mm scale. Anatomy reference only, NOT a North American lineage ID.
items.caption: Close-up of the Phragmites leaf blade/sheath collar from Austria. The fine fringe at the collar is visible above the pale sheath; the 5-mm image scale is from the original photographer. Native North American americanus generally has a 1–1.7 mm ligule versus ~0.4–0.9 mm in introduced Eurasian populations, but this photographed plant is not a measured lineage comparison.
items.why_it_matters: Crews can locate the real ligule and hairy collar before collecting a calibrated same-stem measurement; not suitable for declaring a Texas plant native or invasive.
